content: The guidelines are informed by a range of evidence, including biological and behavioral rationales, as well as additional resources developed by Member States and global partners. These guidelines focus on the use of multiple micronutrient powders (MNPs) for point-of-use fortification of foods consumed by infants and young children aged 6–23 months and children aged 2–12 years. Dissemination of the guidelines will occur through a broad network of international partners, including WHO country and regional offices, ministries of health, WHO collaborating centers, universities, other United Nations agencies, and nongovernmental organizations. The guidelines will also be published in the WHO Reproductive Health Library. The WHO Department of Nutrition for Health and Development will disseminate the guidelines through coordinated efforts with the six WHO regional offices, training workshops for health workers at national and regional levels, and presentations at scientific forums on both national and international scales. The guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations to Member States on the effects and safety of using MNPs for point-of-use food fortification for infants and children. These recommendations aim to assist Member States in making informed decisions about interventions that best suit their specific contexts, needs, resources, and ongoing programs. If Member States choose to adopt these recommendations, they must assess the policy implications of their decisions. Implementation considerations include evaluating baseline caregiver awareness and knowledge of MNPs to identify misconceptions and prevent misuse. Behavior-change communication strategies should account for the time it may take individuals to adopt the use of MNPs in their daily lives. Household visits can reinforce accurate information, address questions about preparation and side effects, and promote acceptance and adherence. A robust baseline survey or database on the prevalence of micronutrient deficiencies and dietary intake is essential for program planning. Data should be disaggregated to identify health inequities across population groups, which is also critical for monitoring. WHO has developed tools such as the WHO Handbook on health inequality monitoring and the Health Equity Assessment Toolkit (HEAT) to support Member States in assessing within-country health inequalities. The guidelines emphasize the importance of a human rights-based approach during implementation to protect the rights of children. Ethical considerations are particularly relevant in malaria-endemic settings due to potential interactions and adverse effects of increased iron intake. Coordination with public health measures to prevent, diagnose, and treat malaria is essential to avoid unintended harm and ensure health benefits. Monitoring and evaluation are integral to the implementation process. A specific manual for setting up a monitoring system for MNPs has been developed by HF-TAG. Member States are encouraged to develop plans with appropriate indicators, including disaggregated data for health-equity monitoring. WHO has also developed a generic logic model for micronutrient interventions in public health, which Member States can adapt for designing, implementing, monitoring, and evaluating nutrition programs. The WHO Vitamin and Mineral Nutrition Information System (VMNIS) micronutrient database has been in place since 1991 to assess the micronutrient status of populations, monitor the impact of strategies, and track trends over time. The Evidence and Programme Guidance Unit of the Department of Nutrition for Health and Development manages this database in collaboration with national health authorities. For global-level evaluation, WHO has created a centralized platform for sharing information on nutrition actions in public health practice. This platform supports the monitoring and evaluation of public health programs implementing micronutrient interventions.
